system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2160-01-30 08:45:00 to 2160-02-02 19:43:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

Discharge Instructions:
1. Please return to the emergency department or notify your 
physician if you experience any of the following: severe pain 
not relieved by medication, increased swelling, decreased 
sensation, difficulty with movement, fevers greater than 101.5, 
shaking chills, increasing redness or drainage from the incision 
site, chest pain, shortness of breath or any other concerns.

2. Please follow up with your primary physician regarding this 
admission and any new medications and refills. 

3. Resume your home medications unless otherwise instructed.

4. You have been given medications for pain control. Please do 
not drive, operate heavy machinery, or drink alcohol while 
taking these medications. As your pain decreases, take fewer 
tablets and increase the time between doses. This medication can 
cause constipation, so you should drink plenty of water daily 
and take a stool softener (such as colace) as needed to prevent 
this side effect.  Call your surgeons office 3 days before you 
are out of medication so that it can be refilled.  These 
medications cannot be called into your pharmacy and must be 
picked up in the clinic or mailed to your house.  Please allow 
an extra 2 days if you would like your medication mailed to your 
home.

5. You may not drive a car until cleared to do so by your 
surgeon.

6. Please keep your wounds clean. You may shower starting five 
(5) days after surgery, but no tub baths or swimming for at 
least four (4) weeks. No dressing is needed if wound continues 
to be non-draining. Any stitches or staples that need to be 
removed will be taken out at your follow-up visit in three (3) 
weeks after your surgery.

7. Please call your surgeon's office to schedule or confirm your 
follow-up appointment in three (3) weeks.

8. Please DO NOT take any non-steroidal anti-inflammatory 
medications (NSAIDs such as celebrex, ibuprofen, advil, aleve, 
motrin, etc).

9. ANTICOAGULATION: Please continue your lovenox for four (4) 
weeks to help prevent deep vein thrombosis (blood clots).  If 
you were taking aspirin prior to your surgery, it is OK to 
continue at your previous dose while taking this medication.  
___ STOCKINGS x 6 WEEKS.

10. WOUND CARE: Please keep your incision clean and dry. It is 
okay to shower five days after surgery but no tub baths, 
swimming, or submerging your incision until after your four (4) 
week checkup. Please place a dry sterile dressing on the wound 
each day if there is drainage, otherwise leave it open to air. 
Check wound regularly for signs of infection such as redness or 
thick yellow drainage. Staples will be removed at your follow-up 
visit in three (3) weeks.

11. ___ (once at home): Home ___, dressing changes as 
instructed, and wound checks.

12. ACTIVITY: Weight bearing as tolerated on the operative 
extremity. Mobilize. CPM/ROM as tolerated. No strenuous exercise 
or heavy lifting until follow up appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You’re here today for your left total knee replacement, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been in so much pain for months. I hope this helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expect it will. Your imaging shows severe degeneration, so the surgery should relieve a lot of that pressure and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a little nervous. I’ve had a lot of health issues—my kidney transplant, the stroke, and seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your history carefully. You’re on tacrolimus and other meds we’re monitoring. The anesthesia team is aware of your epilepsy and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my allergies—penicillin, azathioprine, cephalosporins. I don’t want to get anything that could react.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. You’ll get vancomycin and clindamycin for antibiotic prophylaxis—both safe for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. When will the surgery be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Scheduled for 12 PM. We’ll take you up shortly. Any other questions before then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m ready. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, it’s Dr. Lee again. Surgery went well—your new knee is in place, no complications. You tolerated everything well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My leg feels heavy, but not painful yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started a PCA pump so you can control pain with a button. Nurses will monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on that all week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually just overnight. Tomorrow we’ll switch to oral meds if you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your hemoglobin dropped—HCT was 17, now 19.5 after two units of blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit weak. Is that from the blood loss?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, surgery causes some blood loss. We gave you two units yesterday, and you’ll get two more today because your pressure dipped and urine output was low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More transfusions? Is that safe with my kidney?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted nephrology. They agree it’s necessary. Your creatinine is elevated at 3.4, but we’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my urine test showed an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, E. coli in your urine. But it’s sensitive to Bactrim, which we’re starting today—should clear it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had UTIs before since my transplant. Hope this one doesn’t last long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With treatment, it shouldn’t. We’ll repeat the culture to make sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your HCT is now 22.7—much better. We’ll hold off on more blood. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I’m on pills now, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, acetaminophen and a little hydromorphone as needed. We also started Lovenox this morning for blood clot prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard those can cause bleeding. Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Risk is low, especially with your current labs. We’ll monitor. You’ll also wear compression stockings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And physical therapy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll see you today. Goal is to get you up and moving, weight-bearing as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: PT was tough. My leg’s stiff, but I walked a few steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. Keep working with them. Your incision looks clean, no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I saw some drainage earlier. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A small amount of sanguinous staining is expected. We changed the dressing—wound is intact.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re doing well. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? What about the blood thinner?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Lovenox for four weeks. Also starting warfarin. We’ll check your INR in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Warfarin? I’ve heard that’s tricky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, but we’ll monitor. Avoid leafy greens suddenly changing your intake, and no NSAIDs like ibuprofen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume all your home medications—tacrolimus, furosemide, metoprolol, etc. We’ve updated your list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Bactrim for the UTI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, take it for seven days. Drink plenty of water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I see the surgeon again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In three weeks. Staples will be removed then. Call to schedule if you haven’t already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, starting five days post-op—so tomorrow. Just no soaking in a tub or swimming for four weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain meds? I don’t want to get constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added senna and multivitamins. Take hydromorphone only as needed. Increase intervals as pain improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t drive, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not until cleared by your surgeon. Use your cane or walker as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Go to the ER or call us if you have fever over 101.5, increased redness, swelling, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m nervous but ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great. Home health will help with dressing changes and PT. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I watch for signs of blood clots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—swelling, pain, or redness in the leg. Also chest pain or shortness of breath. Those need immediate attention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the mupirocin ointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use it in your nose twice a day for five days to prevent infection. It’s a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Any new pain or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel stable. Leg’s sore but manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Remember—weight-bearing as tolerated, keep the wound clean, and follow up in three weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for a left total knee replacement due to severe degenerative joint disease. The surgery was performed on 2160-01-30 and proceeded without complications. Postoperatively, she developed acute posthemorrhagic anemia requiring four units of packed red blood cells over two days. Her renal function was closely monitored given her history of kidney transplant, and she was seen by nephrology. A urinary tract infection caused by E. coli, sensitive to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, was identified and treated. Pain was managed initially with a PCA pump, transitioning to oral acetaminophen and hydromorphone. She received Lovenox for DVT prophylaxis and was started on warfarin at discharge with instructions for INR monitoring. Physical therapy began on postoperative day one, and she achieved weight-bearing as tolerated. The wound was clean and healing without signs of infection. She was discharged home with home health services and detailed instructions on wound care, anticoagulation, and follow-up.
